lines.text: That hinge has been off since the spring gales. I have the pin. I have the hammer.
Ask me about the hinge again next year and I will say this, in this tone, holding this cup.
My back. We are not going to discuss my back.
Somebody has been at the honey and I have narrowed it down to four people.
Two more baskets and then I sit down. I have said that twice already today.
The wind turns at about four. You can set the whole afternoon by it if you pay attention.
I want one day where nothing needs mending. One. I am not asking for a week.
The pump is fine. The pump has been fine for six years in the way that a thing about to break is fine.
Crates are packed and still stacked because the cart has a wheel off. One wheel. Six weeks.
That is my sister's shelf. Leave it as it is, please.
We are out of good nails, so today everything gets bad nails and a bit of hope.
Bread went wrong this morning. Same flour, same oven, same hands. No idea.

We moved up in my mother's time. Everybody has a moving-up in their family somewhere.
That was a street. Where the water is flat, there. That whole line was a street.

My grandfather learned to swim in a spot that is now forty strokes out from the shore.
The frogs move up a year before we do. It is not superstition, it is just that they are quicker.

Every family here has a house their grandparents built that you would need a boat to visit.
The old road runs down and into the water and keeps going, straight, for a good way.

My father cries when it rains hard and calls it the wind, and we all let him have the wind.
There is a bowl in this house with a blue bird on it that came out of somebody else's kitchen.

It is probably not true. It is also the reason two families here get out of bed. So.

They will not find it. Not because it is hidden. Because there is nothing to find.
The ring of arches was a cistern, everyone says. We tell the children lions drank there.
Lions drank at the arches. Everyone knows that. Nobody has produced a lion.
The carved city was cut from the rock rather than built, so it is held to be older than the water.
Which would mean there was a before. That is what the argument is actually about, every time.

Build like the mountain terraces and you live. That is the whole of upland thinking, in one sentence.

Somebody chalked a marker line on the mill wall as though chalk would hold the water off.

I make the children copy pages until their hands cramp and I tell them exactly why, and they still hate it.
We are teaching everyone letters. Everyone. Including people who will never write a word.
The seeds go in wax at the back of the cold chamber. That set is not for us.

Whoever built that shelf measured a future and made furniture for it. I think about it often.
Half of us want to go higher and half of us want to stay and both halves are right, which is the problem.
The ones who went up send word back saying come up. Nobody who stayed has sent word saying stay.
Devi planted the whole row knowing she will be gone before it fruits.

I have opinions about how much fish we eat and nobody has ever asked me for them.

Wind gets under the floor at the big tides and lifts the whole house about a finger's width.
I have put new legs under this house twice and both times they went in longer. That is the whole history of the place.
You can date a house by counting the rungs added to its ladder. Ours has eleven.
There were four rows out past this one. Now there is us, and then there is the water.
At the big tides the sea comes over the boards and we all lift our feet and keep talking.
The uplanders call us stubborn. We call them cowards. Neither side entirely means it.
You can see roofs under us on a still day. You stop finding that strange after about a year.
We are the last row. The last row has always been somebody. It used to be somebody further out.
Nobody out here says flood. We say the level, or this year, or the tides.
Anzu ties on to a chimney when the wind turns. It was her aunt's chimney, when it had a house under it.
Once a year the tide drops far enough to show the top of the schoolyard fence, and then it covers it again.
The children dare each other to touch it. I did the same at their age. It is only a railing.
I was born in a room that is directly under where we are standing. My mother pointed it out once.
The old well is down there, full of sea water. We call that a joke. It is not one.

We have done that for nineteen years knowing it washes off. That is not stupidity, it is the point.
I can find any doorway under this village by feel, in the dark, with my eyes shut. I have had to.
The brick under the water is a red that nobody fires any more. You can pick out the old walls by colour alone.
There is a boat out here named for a woman who drowned and we all say the name perfectly normally.
We float over houses and argue about a carved city that none of us will ever stand in front of.

I did not rub it off. You do not rub off the thing that got somebody through the winter.
The wall-walkers stop here for salt and not one of them can swim. Not one, in twenty years.
They walk a wall looking for a hole. We bail a house. Everybody has picked something.

Everyone out here agrees the tomb is the most beautiful thing there is. Nobody out here has seen it.
The markers stand on dry land while we stand on sticks. That comes up in every argument eventually.
Some families go up in the spring and some do not, and the two halves have stopped eating together.
Swimming comes before walking here. That is not a boast about our children.
We bail until we cannot bail. Then we go. Not one season before that, whatever anybody says.
The names of the drowned houses are being cut into a roof beam, so the beam carries them out.
The children have to know these walkways by heart, in the dark, in wind. That is not a chore.
My mother announced in front of everybody that she will not move, so now she cannot take it back.

Somebody asked outright how long this row has got. The whole room suddenly had jobs to do.
One of these children will be the one who closes this place up. I know which one. She does too.
Three doors in this village still shut properly. I could take you to all three.

Turning the drying fish is a job for somebody with patience and I have run out of both.
The bell on the post is for weather. It has been rung twice in my life and both times it was right.
The sand gets in whatever anybody does, and we all still shout about it every single day.

Boats tie where the carts used to turn. There is a ring in the wall for each of those.

One more family moves from the bottom row to the top each year. Nobody has ever moved back down.
You can tell how long a house has stood empty by how far the weeds have got up its door.
There is a dark line at the same height on every wall here. That is where it gets to now.
This place has been halfway through leaving for as long as anybody has been standing in it.
We are mid-decision. I know how that sounds. We have been mid-decision for four years.

Nine terraces, both sides, weeded by hand. Ask me how my afternoon is going.

Sums in the morning and letters after, every day, for every child, no exceptions.

Four stones, two trees. She is under the smaller one, and the smaller one is the one that fruits.

The old road climbs up here and then stops at nothing, because the something is under water.
We can see the stilt village from here. They are on sticks. We are on rock. They think we are cowards.
The terraces are cut so the rain runs off without taking the soil. That was copied from somewhere else.
The ledger lists every house lost, the year it went, the family, and what they managed to save.
It does not say that one of them sang while she gutted fish, in a voice like a gull with a grievance.
Nobody was measuring the singing. That is the part that gets me about the ledger.
My great-grandmother carried plum stones up here in her mouth because both hands were full.
Four stones, two trees. She is under the smaller one and the smaller one is the one that fruits.
There are keys hanging by our door for houses that have been underwater since before my mother.
One whole shelf of the ledger is a single year. One year. One shelf.
We keep a chair that came up from the low house. Nobody sits in it. Nobody will move it either.
Our terraces copy the mountain place, where they built well and did not drown.
We copied a drawing of a drawing, my grandfather says, and he says it with real feeling.
The record keeper argues the carved city with anyone who sits down at his table.
Carved, not built, therefore older than the water, therefore the world had a before. That is his whole case.
He is right. He is also the reason people eat standing up in his house.
The pointy markers all stand on high ground, which people say proves the builders knew what high ground was.
The calendar stone is supposed to predict the water. My teacher says it predicts nothing at all.
She says that quietly, and only to us, and never when there are pilgrims in the village.
Everybody is copying books. Two of everything, then four. My hand cramps and I have complained formally.
The answer I got was: somebody has to be able to read this in fifty years. That shut me up.
We are writing the names of the drowned villages down before the last person who saw them dies.
There are four such people left. Four. That number is why everybody is in such a hurry.
They planted an entire orchard this spring that fruits in nine years. Somebody did that sum on purpose.
The seed jars go into the cave where it is cold. Not to eat. To keep.
There is already a plan for where the stilt families go when they come up. Nobody has shown them the plan.
Nobody has told the lowlanders that. It would be an insult and it is also a kindness.
My mother says our job is remembering. It is a strange thing to be handed as a job.
Thin air, thin soup, thin walls. That is the joke here and it is still the joke.
Ice on the bucket most mornings. We only properly wash on the warm days.
The path down takes two hours and the path up takes four and it is the same path.
We burn dung because nothing grows tall enough to burn at this height.
Bringing the animals in before dark is my job and dark is very early up here.
There is nothing to farm, so people keep records instead. That is an actual answer people give.
I sleep next to the dog for the warmth and my mother has decided not to know about it.
From up here you can see the whole coast and it is a different shape from the map in the hall.
Nobody up here worries about the level. That is the entire reason there are people up here.
If it reaches us, my father says, it has reached everybody, so it will not be our problem alone.
The traders tell us which villages went under this year. It is a short list and it is never empty.
There is a map nailed up in the hall with a lot of it now simply wrong.
Nobody redraws it. Somebody just pencils in the new edge every few years, over the old one.
We came up two lifetimes ago and everybody still calls my family the new ones.
The dead go into the rock because you cannot dig a grave in ground like this.
There is a niche in the wall with a comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth in it.
Nothing labels them. Somebody put them there, and then that somebody died as well.
My grandmother came up from a fishing village and has not touched a boat in fifty years.
There is a boat up here. On a mountain. Somebody carried it up and nobody living knows why.
The oldest names in the record are all from one drowned place, all in the same handwriting.
We eat out of a bowl from a house nobody alive has been inside. It is a good bowl.
My grandfather still ties knots the coast way and has not seen the coast since before I was born.
We are as high as the mountain terrace place and half as clever. My grandfather's line, not mine.
Pilgrims come up wanting salt. Always salt. It is for the walk along the great wall.
They are looking for the break where the sea supposedly came through. They have looked for generations.
There is no break. My mother says that at home and never says it where a pilgrim can hear.
Somebody up here owns a drawing of the carved city and charges people to look at it.
It is a bad drawing. It is also the only one, so he is doing very well out of it.
The calendar stone is meant to say when the water stops. Every pilgrim reads it differently and goes home certain.
The tomb is the one thing they all agree on. Even the arguing ones go quiet about the tomb.
We take in whoever comes up. There is a room kept ready and it is rarely empty for long.
Nobody asks new arrivals what they left behind. That is not politeness, it is a rule.
The record book has run out of pages twice and they made more pages both times.
I am learning the old hand, the difficult one, so the earliest pages do not go silent.
They are copying everything into two sets and one set goes deep into the cave, in the dry.
We are planting trees at this height for the first time ever. Nobody knows if they will take.
The oldest man here wants to be carried down to see the sea once before he dies.
Nobody has said yes and nobody has said no, and he is not getting any lighter.
It is the same temperature in here all year. Outside changes constantly. In here does not.
Trimming the lamps is my job. The soot has built a black stripe along the roof of the passage.
The stripe is thickest at the height of a walking adult, which tells you how long people have walked it.
Water drips into a stone basin and fills it by morning, every morning, at the same rate.
The basin is worn into the rock. That is not carving. That is just the drip, taking its time.
The floor of the front chamber has been swept so long it now sits dished in the middle.
Nobody goes past the third lamp without telling somebody. That is the only real rule down here.
People have lived in here longer than anywhere else. Longer than the villages by a lot.
The old entrance is underwater now. Fish go in and out of it. We use the upper one.
Things come in here when the low villages give up on keeping them dry.
They moved the seed jars deeper in after a wet winter, because deeper is drier.
There is a water mark on the wall from a flood so old nobody knows which flood it was.
Everybody's grandparents' things end up in here eventually. Ours are on the fourth shelf along.
The stone does not change. People say that constantly, and they say it like it is a comfort.
It is not a comfort. It just means the stone is not the thing that is moving.
The dead lie in the fourth chamber with their feet towards the entrance. All of them, the same way.
The oldest lie deepest, so walking in is walking backwards through everybody.
There is a niche holding a comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth, and no name anywhere near it.
Three people, or one person's whole life. Nobody can tell any more, and that is the point of it.
Read along the jar labels and the writing changes halfway down the shelf. Same shelf, two people, decades apart.
The first hand stopped. The second hand carried on. Nobody has ever explained that to me.
Books are stacked spine out in the dry chamber and the ones about the sea are read to pieces.
Somebody copied an entire book into the margins of another book, having run out of paper.
There are ochre handprints along the low passage at the height of a walking adult.
One line of them is smaller and lower and keeps stopping, which is a child keeping up.
Seven shapes are painted in a row on the deep wall: a triangle, a long line, a ring of arches, and four more.
Everyone agrees the triangle is the markers and the line is the great wall. After that it is a fight.
There is a charcoal drawing of the ring of arches with a water line ruled dead straight across it.
Under the line somebody has written a number. Nobody agrees what the number counts.
People bring their worst arguments down here. The echo does something to them and everybody leaves more certain than they came.
Carved, not built. Say it in the dark and it comes back sounding like proof, which is the trick.
A calendar of small squares is cut into the rock by the entrance and the squares run out four winters back.
Whoever was cutting them stopped. Nobody has picked it up. Everybody walks past it every day.
The seed jars are in two sets now. The back set is sealed with wax and is not for us.
I asked who the back set is for and got the longest silence of my life.
There is a new shelf down here, planed smooth and pegged in, completely empty, built to fit books.
Built to fit books that have not been written. Somebody measured a future and made a shelf for it.
The copying is done in here because it is dry. Two of everything, then four, then deeper in.
They are teaching me the way out in the dark, by hand, by count of turns. That is a lesson now.
I can do a flip. A proper one, off the top, all the way over. I'm not doing it now though.
Ravi says if you eat the eyes you can see in the dark. I've eaten four. Nothing yet.
There's a bird that comes when it's going to rain. Grey, cross-looking, one leg shorter than the other. Her name is Betta. I named her, so it is.
I'm not scared of the big crabs. I am careful of them. That is a different thing and my mother agrees with me.
We're not allowed to play the shouting game near the mending. So we play it just far enough off that it doesn't count as near.
Meera says her hair grew long in one night. It didn't. I saw it the day before and it was exactly the same hair.
My job is stones. I pick the stones out of the beans. It is the worst job there is and I am extremely good at it.
Tan can whistle through his teeth and I can't. I have been practising eleven days. It comes out as breath.
If you hold still long enough a lizard will walk on you. I got one up to my elbow before I laughed and ruined it.
It never rains inside and the back part is never cold. When it's blowing out there you can hear it at the mouth and it can't get in. Best place there is.
My voice goes down the long bit and comes back different. Deeper. Like somebody much bigger is agreeing with me.
There are jars along the wall taller than me, full of seeds, and I'm not to touch them. So I count them instead. Forty-one. I have counted it wrong before.
In the morning the bucket has a lid of ice on it and you can lift the whole lid off in one piece. That is my job. Nobody else is allowed.
I keep the fire from dark until food. Small ones first, then the big one at the end. It has not gone out on me. Not once.
We eat the same thing at the same time every day. Once there was honey, and I can tell you exactly where I was sitting.
There are seven empty houses and I have been inside six. The last one has a wasp thing in the roof and I am waiting for winter.
We keep saying we're going. My mother says it in the morning. Then at night she goes out and plants something.
The house with no roof is the best house. The rain comes straight in and you can stand in it and nobody says get out of the rain.
They make us say the year list. Every name, in order, back and back. Get one wrong and you start again from the front. Meera never gets one wrong and it makes me want to bite her.
I built a wall of my own. It's small. It fell over twice and then it stayed up, and now it holds four beans in.
The goats know their own names and I do not know all of theirs. That is embarrassing for me and I am working on it.
You write the numbers in the book with the good ink, and if you blot it you go and sit outside. I have sat outside twice.
Our whole house moves a bit. It isn't broken, it's meant to. When the wind is up my bed swings and I pretend it's a fight I'm winning.
You dive off the corner post, not the middle. The middle has the anchor rope under it and the rope takes your skin off. Everybody knows that. Ravi didn't.
I bail before food and after food. Two buckets each time. My arms are getting big. Feel them. No, properly.
There's a fish that lives under our floor. Fat, striped, sulky. My father says catch it. I say she lives there, so no.
My grandmother's kitchen is under the water. I've been in it. There's a shelf and the shelf still has a pot on it, sideways, and it stays like that.
People from up the hill come down and look at the water and go quiet. It's just the water. It's been doing that the whole time. I don't know what they're looking for.
I'm going to be the best swimmer of anyone ever. That's easy. The ones before me had all that ground to walk about on, so they got no practice.
When I'm old the water will be up at the tall tree. I worked it out on my fingers. So I'll live above the tall tree. I've thought about it, it's fine.
Everything good is at the bottom. Cups and combs and doors. That's where the old people kept their things, at the bottom, and that is why it's all under now.
You can tell how old a wall is by how wet it is. The wettest wall is the oldest wall. I worked that out myself and nobody has said no yet.
My father says don't go past the second post. So I go to the second post and put my hand on it and look, and that isn't past.
There's a bell out there somewhere and the sea has got it. Nobody agrees where. I say everybody should shut up at the same time and listen, and nobody will do it.
The dead are all in the back in the jars, and I'm meant to be quiet in there, but I sing, because the sound goes round and round and they have heard worse.
This cave has never been wet. Not one time, not in anybody's anybody's time. So it is the winning place. And it's still just a cave.
There are seeds in here for growing things that don't grow here any more. I asked when we're planting them. Nobody said a number.
From up here the sea is just a shine along the bottom of everything. You can't see it doing anything. It is, though. Very slowly, which is the sneaky way.
The first ones who came up here carried doors on their backs. Actual doors. I don't know what they were going to put them in, but they weren't leaving them behind.
Nobody will ever have to move from here, my grandfather says. Then he goes out and looks down at the water and comes back in. Every day. Same time.
I walked down to the water once with my brother. Two days there. The bottom is warm and loud and crowded and everything smells of something. I want to live there.
That house drank last winter. It took some in and then it sat down. It had been empty for ages before that, but I still say sorry when I go past.
We're moving. We have been moving for two years. The cart is packed and the goat is ready and my mother keeps finding one more thing that has to be done first.
Half our garden went salty. The salty half goes grey and crunchy and you can snap a whole plant with your foot. That's the only good part of it.
Nobody fixes anything here any more. If a shutter goes, it goes. My father says there's no sense putting a good hinge on a house you're leaving. Then he oils the hinge.
My aunt's tree is standing in the sea up past its knees and it still has leaves on. She's dead and the tree isn't. I said that out loud and got told off.
We came up in my mother's mother's time, before anybody I know. So I have never had to go anywhere. I would quite like to have to.
There's a book with where the water got to written in it, every year, going back and back and back. I'm allowed to turn the pages if my hands are dry.
They cut this hill into steps because there's a place far off cut into steps and that place stayed up. Ours keep falling down. So either we're doing it wrong or that place is lying.
The ones down on the water call us runners and they laugh when they say it. My uncle laughs back. Then he's quiet for a bit after.
That was a street down there. My mother walked on it. Now I swim over it, and swimming is better than walking, so I don't know what she's sad about.
You can see our old door on a still day. Green, with the bar across. I go down and touch it every summer. It's a rule I made.
We put the floor higher last winter. Everything came out, then the boards went up on the blocks, then everything went back in. Four days. I carried the small things.
There's a whole roof under our boat and in summer the fish sit on it like it's theirs. Which it is now, I suppose. I'd let them.
The hill people won't sleep over water. They say it's mad. I say sleeping on a hill is mad, because nothing moves at all, so how do you get off to sleep?
I can get to the bottom of the well house in one breath. Ravi gets halfway and comes up saying he swallowed something. He always swallows something.
My aunt's window is the round one with the bars. Mama says don't go in. I go to the bars and look and then I come back up, so that is not going in.
Everyone gets sad about the old town. I have only ever seen it wet. It is better wet. There are fish in the doorways and you can swim through a window like a bird.
Tan is scared of the deep bit. I told him the deep bit is just a road. He said roads don't have eels in. They do now.
I know four names of dead people and one of them is a boat.
Meera says her grandmother's chair is still down there facing the same way it always faced. I dived and it isn't a chair. I didn't tell her.
Grown-ups say the word before like it's a place you could walk to. Before, before, before. I say it too but I don't know where it is.
I'm hungry. That's it. That's the thing I wanted to say.
My name was somebody else's first and she is dead. Everybody says I have her chin. So I have got a dead lady's chin, which is not my fault.
The best thing about a drowned house is you go in through the roof. No door. You just fall in very slowly and land on the ceiling from the wrong side.
There's a bell down there somewhere. I've never heard it ring. But if you go all the way down and hold still and stop your ears wobbling, you nearly do.
Great-gran is in the third room in a niche with her name scratched over the top. We take her a bit of bread on her day. She doesn't eat it. Somebody eats it.
The jars have seeds in from before anybody. If you shake one you get shouted at by four adults at the same time, which I know because I did it.
The names go all the way round the room and then start again in a row above, and then again above that. Three rows. They keep having to start higher.
From the flat rock you can count roofs down in the water. Today there were nine. Some days it's six, because the light is wrong, not because the roofs went anywhere.

Papa carried me up here in a basket when I was small. He tells it like it was the hardest thing anyone ever did. I don't remember it, so as far as I'm concerned I have always been up here and he can stop.
It's cold, there's no fish, and the goat hates everybody. But from our door you can see the whole water at once. Down there they can only see the bit they're standing in.
Mama says everyone carries something when we go. I said I'll carry the cat. Now I have to carry the cat, and the cat has opinions, so that was a mistake.
The blue house has nobody in it so we made it ours. There's a mark on the doorframe where somebody measured a kid. The kid got taller than me and then went away.
People take the doors with them when they leave. Just the doors. So there are houses standing there with holes where the doors were and you can walk straight in and nobody minds.
Everyone here is going and nobody has gone. They talk about it at every single meal. I said just go then, and got sent outside, and outside was better anyway.

They write the water down in a book every week. One line, one number. It is the most boring book there is. But our old road is in it, and the road isn't anywhere now, so the book has more road than the world does.
I have never touched the sea. I've looked at it every day of my whole life and never once touched it. When I say that to the raft kids they laugh until they fall over.
Grandpa is on page eleven. Just his name, the year, and a little sum at the end. That's all a person gets in there. He was much bigger than a line.
Our raft is Perla. Perla was Mama's sister and she went under with a boat, and now she is a raft, which is better than being nothing. I'm not allowed to say that at supper.
Under our floorboards there's a chimney. On a still day when the water goes clear you can see right down it. Nothing ever comes out. I've watched for ages.
The green door still has its handle on. I go down and hold the handle and turn it and it turns, every time, and then my chest starts going and I have to come up.
Bailing is boring but I'm the fastest at it, and being fastest at a boring thing is still being fastest.
The pointy ones are markers. People built them long ago because they knew, and they put the top exactly where the water stops. So when it gets to the top it stops. That's what a marker is for.
There's a hole in the Wall. That's why all this happened. When somebody finds the hole and plugs it, the water goes back down and everyone goes home and I get my own room.
The round one is a cup. It held the drinking water for everybody, and the lions drank there too, down at the low end, because a lion would empty your bucket in one go.

Nobody built Petra. They took rock away instead of piling it up, which is backwards. And you cannot carve a rock underwater, so it was before the water, so there was a before. Ravi says there wasn't. Ravi is an idiot.
The counting stone tells you the water. You read the corners and it gives you a year. Old Neru says it says nothing, but Old Neru can't read the corners, he just looks at them.
The white one is a tomb for one person. One. A whole building for one dead lady. Everybody agrees about it, and everybody never agrees about anything, so it must be true.
There are seven big things and they are all still standing, and every little thing is under. So little things drown and big things don't. I worked that out by myself.
The steps place is how you're meant to build. Flat bit, wall, flat bit, wall, all the way up a mountain. If we'd built like that we'd be fine. We built like idiots.

I'm going to make a wonder. It will have steps, and a hole for the water to go in, and my name cut into the front, and it will still be standing when every single other thing is under.
People argue about all of them except the white tomb. You say the white tomb and everybody goes quiet and nods, even the two who won't share a fire.
The wonders don't leak. That's the whole thing about them. Our roof is four years old and it leaks in two places, and theirs is a thousand years old and it doesn't.
The Wall held it all back once, like a bowl holds soup. Then it cracked. I've never seen a crack that big, but it's a very long wall and people give up in the middle.
There's a book down here with all seven drawn in it and two pages torn out, so there might have been nine. Nobody will say which two are missing. I think they don't know either.

Somebody scratched a little pointy one on the wall by the seed room, low down, where a kid would reach. It's older than my grandmother's grandmother. So a kid did that ages ago and then died, and the scratch is still going.
Up here is like the steps place. Flat bits and walls, only colder and worse. Build like that and you live, they say, usually while somebody's toes are going black.
The pilgrims come over the pass in spring in terrible boots, off to walk the Wall. They ask which way and we point and they go. None of them has ever come back over the pass the other way.

Pilgrims came through wanting bread and we gave them some. They're walking the whole Wall looking for the break in it. They've been walking six years. I asked if they'd found it yet and one of them looked at me for a long time.

The book has a drawing of the pointy ones with the water line marked along the side. Different people marked different lines. There are four lines on it now. They can't all be the right one.

On a clear evening from our roof there's a bump on the edge of the water, right at the end. Mama says it's a cloud. It is not a cloud. Clouds move and that has never moved once.
When they plug the Wall the water goes down and our house will be standing up in the air on its legs like a bird. Then we'll need stairs. Proper stairs, to the ground.

Ravi says a lion swims past the poles at night. Lions drank at the round place and the round place is days away, so it would have to be a very good swimmer. I still don't go out past the poles at night.
They keep asking each other whether it's worth teaching us letters. I'm sat right there. I can hear them. So now I'm learning out of spite and I'm going to be extremely good at it.
Everyone says the water stops when it reaches the markers. Then they say maybe. I don't mind which, I just want to be told once and have it stay told.
When I'm grown I'll have a house with three floors and I'll use the top one for nothing at all. Just an empty room. That's what being grown is.
Grown ups have a face for when I ask how long. It's the same face on all of them, every time. They must go somewhere and practise it together.
I know the letters up to M and after that it goes silly. Two of them make the same noise. Whoever did it should have stopped while it was going well.
Mum says learn to read so you can tell them. Tell who. She says the ones after us. There's no after, there's just us and then more of us, which is the same thing.
I'm the best swimmer of anyone my size, which is useful, and reading isn't. I'm doing both anyway because otherwise Gran does the wobbly voice.
The old ones talk about going up like it's an enormous decision. We go up all the time. We went up before I was born and I turned out fine.
I asked what we do when there's no more up. Everyone laughed. It wasn't a joke, so now I don't know if they know either.
My name went in the big book the day I was born and that's the only time I've been in it. I'm getting in it again for something better. Something with jumping.
I can hold my breath while they count to forty. Nobody counts fairly. I want a proper count, by someone who isn't Ravi, with everybody watching, and then we'll see.
Everything was decided by people who are dead. Dad says that when he's cross. I'm going to decide loads of things and then be dead and everyone can be cross at me.
I'm learning letters and Ravi's learning knots. We agree knots are better. The problem with knots is you can't tell anybody anything with them.
There's a word grown ups start and then don't finish. They get two sounds into it and then have a drink. I've got the two sounds. I'm collecting the rest.
Nobody's coming. I heard that said. It was said flat, the way you say there's no more salt. I don't think anyone was expecting anyone, so it's fine.
The jars hold seeds from before anyone. You're not to open them. I opened one. It was seeds. I put them back and I have told nobody, so keep it in your mouth.
Great-aunt Sura is in the wall with a bowl beside her. We put a bit of dinner in it on her day. She doesn't eat it. Something eats it. I think it's Uncle.
People have been in this cave the whole time, always, no gap. That's what gets said when someone brings up climbing higher. Then everyone looks at the floor and puts more wood on.
I do my letters in the dust on the low shelf, because paper is for the proper writing. Rubbing them out leaves a shine. My name is shiny in four places down there.
It's never cold in here and never hot. Outside can do whatever it's doing. In here it's just today, same as it was for Sura, same as it'll be for the next lot.
There are more books than there are people. Loads more. Somebody is meant to learn to read them all before they go soft, and everyone keeps looking at the small ones, which is unfair.
From our door the sea looks flat and grey like a slate. You can't see it doing anything. It is doing something, everyone says so, but from here it just lies there like the goat.
There's nowhere higher than us. I checked with Dad. He said there's the peak. I said nobody can live on the peak, and he said no, and we ate the beans.
We burn the chairs when it gets very cold. The small ones first. I'm not allowed to say aloud which chair is next, because Gran is sitting in it.
Somebody walks down every spring to see who's still out on the water. Last spring he came back with a girl and no news. The girl eats an enormous amount.
I'm learning letters because there's nothing else to do in winter. My A is good. My G is a snail. Mum says a snail is fine so long as somebody can read it in a hundred years.
We used to have two goats. Ask about the other goat. Actually don't, Gran's just there, and she does a face.
They packed the pots, then unpacked them, then packed them again. I sit on the basket now so it isn't my fault when we don't go.
The house with the blue door is mine because nobody has said it isn't. I keep shells along the windowsill. When we go I'll leave them, and someone will think a person lives there.
Everyone who moves up says they'll come down for the fire night. None of them have. I've stopped saving them a place, and Mum saw me not do it, and she said nothing.
Grandma won't go up. She says her knees. Dad says her knees are an excuse, and then he goes quiet, and then he starts mending something that wasn't broken.
There are more doorways than doors here now. I run through every one of them without stopping. My record is nine before I have to breathe.
They teach the letters in the empty house because it has the biggest room and nobody to bother. We sit on the floor where a bed was. You can still see where the bed was.
I write the number in the book every morning. It's mostly the same number. When it changes they read it out twice, as if reading it twice makes it into a different number.
We came up three lots of grandparents ago, which means we're clever, which is what we say when the raft people visit. Then we give them all our dry blankets and don't mention it again.
They're teaching everyone letters now, even the tiny ones. Grandad says somebody has to be able to read the books after. After what. He goes to fetch water when I ask that.
Our terraces are copied off the stone city over the water. Ours slump. Grandad says theirs were made by better hands, then he goes and stacks the stones the same wrong way.
